content: Asthma is the most prevalent chronic medical condition in children and a frequent cause of hospitalisation. Observational studies have suggested that swimming may be an ideal form of physical activity to enhance physical fitness and reduce the burden of asthma. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of swimming training as an intervention for children and adolescents aged 18 years and under with asthma. The review included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared swimming training with usual care, non-physical activity, or physical activities other than swimming. Eight studies involving 262 participants with stable asthma, ranging from mild to severe, were included. Participants were aged between 5 and 18 years. Swimming training programmes varied in duration and frequency, ranging from 30 to 90 minutes per session, two to three times per week, over six to 12 weeks. One study implemented a programme of 30 minutes of swimming training six times per week. The comparison groups included usual care in seven studies and golf in one study. The chlorination status of the swimming pools was not reported in four studies. Two studies used non-chlorinated pools, one used an indoor chlorinated pool, and one used a chlorinated but well-ventilated pool. No statistically significant effects were observed for primary outcomes such as quality of life, asthma control, asthma exacerbations, or corticosteroid use when comparing swimming training with usual care or other physical activities. However, swimming training demonstrated a clinically meaningful improvement in exercise capacity compared to usual care. This was measured as maximal oxygen consumption (VO2 max) during a maximum effort exercise test, with a mean increase of 9.67 mL/kg/min (95% confidence interval [CI] 5.84 to 13.51) in two studies involving 32 participants. When other measures of exercise capacity were pooled across four studies (n = 74), the standardised mean difference (SMD) was 1.34 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.86). Additionally, small increases in resting lung function parameters were observed, with a mean difference (MD) for FEV1 % predicted of 8.07 (95% CI 3.59 to 12.54). These findings were of varying statistical significance. Sensitivity analyses, accounting for risk of attrition bias or the use of imputed standard deviations, did not result in significant changes to the effect sizes. The unknown chlorination status of some pools limited the ability to perform subgroup analyses. Importantly, based on the limited data available, no adverse effects on asthma control or the occurrence of exacerbations were reported. In conclusion, swimming training appears to be well-tolerated in children and adolescents with stable asthma and is associated with improvements in lung function and cardiopulmonary fitness. There was no evidence to suggest that swimming training negatively impacted asthma control in this population. However, the review could not determine whether swimming is superior to other forms of physical activity. Further well-designed trials with larger sample sizes and longer follow-up periods are needed to better understand the long-term benefits of swimming for children and adolescents with asthma.
